rounds.title: Data Modeling & Low-Level Design
rounds.note: Every question in this round asks for the same four parts: (A) requirements, volumes, latency and reporting use cases; (B) a model: entities, keys, facts and dimensions with their grain, star or snowflake, SCD types, history, and OLTP vs OLAP forms; (C) system behaviour: creation, modification, cancellation, concurrency, duplicates, refund consistency and audit; (D) at least two SQL queries against your own model.

rounds.title: Distributed Systems & High-Level Design
rounds.note: Every question in this round expects: (A) ingestion: event schema, topics, partition keys, producer reliability, ordering; (B) stream processing: engine choice, event time against processing time, windows, watermarks, late data, state, exactly-once and its limits; (C) storage and serving; (D) reliability and scale: skew, failures, backpressure, checkpointing, replay, multi-region; (E) explicit trade-offs among latency, consistency, throughput, cost, availability and operational complexity. No single architecture is "the" answer. You are scored on whether your choices are defensible.

rounds.title: Leadership & Architectural Deep Dive
rounds.note:
How to answer. For experience questions, use STAR (Situation, Task, Action, Result) with measurable evidence. Use a real experience, or say plainly that you have not faced this and reason through it. Do not invent one: interviewers probe, and an honest "I haven't, but here is how I would approach it" scores better than a story that collapses under follow-up. Every question can be answered either way.

Standard probes for every question in this round: What alternatives did you consider? Which metrics supported the decision? What failed? What did you personally contribute? What would you do differently? What was the business impact?

Competencies: correctness · code quality · algorithmic efficiency · SQL proficiency · data modeling quality · distributed-system reasoning · reliability and scalability · trade-off analysis · communication · technical leadership.

questions.title: Rolling fare window over a time-based stream
questions.skills: Monotonic deque, incremental aggregates, boundary semantics, API design
questions.technologies: Python

sections.scenario: RideCo's surge-monitoring service watches every completed trip in a city. For each trip as it arrives, the dashboard shows the highest fare, the average fare and the number of distinct riders over the last W seconds. The window is defined by time, not by a count of events.
sections.problem:
Implement:

class FareWindow:
    def __init__(self, window_seconds: int) -> None: ...
    def add(self, ts: int, rider_id: str, fare_cents: int) -> tuple[int, float, int]:
        """Ingest one event and return (max_fare_cents, avg_fare_cents, distinct_riders)
        over all events with ts in the half-open window (ts - W, ts].
        avg is rounded to 2 decimal places."""

Give a brute-force approach, then an optimised one, then the code, its complexity, and how it handles edge cases.
sections.constraints:
• 1 ≤ W ≤ 86_400; up to 10⁸ events per day per city; 0 ≤ fare_cents ≤ 10⁷.
  • ts is non-decreasing and several events can share one ts. A decreasing ts is an error.
  • add must run in amortised O(1). Memory may be proportional to the number of events inside the window, and no more.
sections.clarifications: Is the window open or closed at each end? What happens to a ts that goes backwards: raise, drop, or buffer? Is a rider with two trips counted once? Do you round half-up or half-to-even?
sections.followups:
1. Events now arrive up to 5 seconds out of order. Keep the answers exact without giving up amortised O(1) for in-order events.
  2. Product also wants the median fare in the window. Give the data structure and its complexity, then say what you would ship instead if the city has 50,000 events per window and an approximate median is acceptable.
sections.criteria: Correct window boundaries; each aggregate maintained incrementally (deque for max, running sum, counted map for distinct); amortised analysis; input validation; clear naming.

tests.name: 200,000 events, ~2,000 in each window, in time (amortised O(1))

questions.title: Shortest burst of net wallet top-ups (refunds allowed)
questions.skills: Seeing why two pointers fail, monotonic deque on prefix sums, proof of correctness, tie-breaking
questions.technologies: Python

sections.scenario: RideCo Wallet lets riders add stored value. One fraud pattern is a fast burst of top-ups funded by stolen cards. The fraudster mixes in small refunds to break naive velocity rules. Risk wants the shortest run of consecutive ledger entries for an account whose net total reaches a threshold.
sections.problem:
def shortest_burst(amounts: list[int], threshold: int) -> tuple[int, int] | None:
    """amounts[i] is a signed ledger entry in cents (top-up > 0, refund < 0), in time order.
    Return (start, end), inclusive indices of the SHORTEST contiguous run with
    sum >= threshold. If several runs are equally short, return the one that starts earliest.
    Return None if no run qualifies."""
sections.constraints: 0 ≤ len(amounts) ≤ 10⁶; -10⁶ ≤ amounts[i] ≤ 10⁶; 1 ≤ threshold ≤ 10¹². If threshold ≤ 0, raise ValueError. Target: O(n) time.
sections.clarifications: Must the run be contiguous in time or just in index order? Does "reaches" mean ≥ or >? Is the input one account's history or interleaved accounts?
sections.followups:
1. Explain why the standard shrinking two-pointer window is wrong when refunds exist. Then give a three-element counterexample.
  2. Make it streaming. Entries arrive one at a time, and you must raise an alert the moment any run that ends at the current entry and is no longer than L entries reaches the threshold. Bound the memory you use.
sections.criteria: Recognises that negatives break monotonicity; derives prefix sums with a monotonic deque; argues correctly why indices can be popped from each end; respects the tie-break; complexity; tests.

tests.name: tie goes to the earliest start
200,000 entries, shortest run ~10,000 long, in time (O(n))

questions.title: Drivers with three or more consecutive rising-earnings trips
questions.skills: Window functions, deterministic ordering, NULL semantics, island detection
questions.technologies: PostgreSQL 16

sections.scenario: An incentives team wants to study drivers on a "hot streak". A streak is three or more consecutive completed trips where each trip earned the driver strictly more than the one before. The trips table holds about 100 million rows (scenario assumption).
sections.problem: Return every maximal streak of length ≥ 3: driver_id, first_trip_id, last_trip_id, trips_in_run, earnings_gain (last minus first earnings). Order the result by driver_id, first_trip_id. Consecutive means consecutive among that driver's completed trips, ordered by completed_at with ties broken by trip_id. Cancelled and no-show trips are ignored and do not break a streak. A completed trip with NULL earnings breaks any streak and cannot belong to one.

questions.title: Deduplicate, then sessionize, rider app events
questions.skills: `DISTINCT ON` or `ROW_NUMBER`, choice of order of operations, inactivity-gap sessions, conversion metrics
questions.technologies: PostgreSQL 16

sections.scenario: The rider app sends events with at-least-once delivery. Retries create duplicate event_ids. Sometimes a retry carries a corrected event_ts after the device clock syncs. Growth wants session-level conversion: did a session contain a trip_requested event?
sections.problem:
• Part A. Deduplicate by event_id, keeping the copy with the latest ingested_at. Then build sessions per rider. A new session starts when the gap since the rider's previous event is more than 30 minutes; a gap of exactly 30 minutes stays in the same session. Return rider_id, session_no (1-based per rider), session_start, session_end, events, converted.
  • Part B. Using Part A, report the daily conversion rate. Attribute each session to the UTC date on which it started. Return session_date, sessions, converted_sessions, conversion_pct (one decimal place).
sections.sample:
CREATE TABLE app_events (
  event_id     TEXT        NOT NULL,   -- NOT unique in this table
  rider_id     BIGINT      NOT NULL,
  event_type   TEXT        NOT NULL,   -- app_open | search | price_view | trip_requested
  event_ts     TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL,
  ingested_at  TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL
);

sections.clarifications: Should the order of events come from device time or ingestion time? Which date owns a session that crosses midnight? Is a 30-minute gap inclusive? Do you deduplicate before sessionizing or after, and does it matter?
sections.followups:
1. Riders are in 400 cities. Product now wants the session date in the rider's local time zone, which can change mid-session when a rider travels. Define the rule and implement it.
  2. This runs hourly over 3 billion events a day, and an event can arrive up to 48 hours late. Design the incremental version. Which sessions must be recomputed when a late event lands, and how do you make the rewrite idempotent?
sections.criteria: Deduplicates before sessionizing, by the specified rule; gap logic matches the inclusive boundary; deterministic tie-break; correct midnight attribution; clean CTE structure.

runner.starter:
-- app_events(event_id, rider_id, event_type, event_ts, ingested_at)
SELECT *
FROM app_events
ORDER BY rider_id, event_ts;

diagnostics.message: Duplicates were not removed: rider 7's first session and rider 9's session each count a retried event twice. Deduplicate by event_id before sessionizing.
You kept the FIRST copy of each event. The rule is the latest ingested_at: e8's corrected timestamp (12:20) keeps rider 9 in one session.
A gap of exactly 30 minutes (08:02 → 08:32) must stay in the same session; only a gap of MORE than 30 minutes starts a new one.

questions.title: Why is the "completed trips by city" query slow?
questions.subtopic: execution plans, partition pruning, correlated subqueries, indexing, skew
questions.skills: Plan reading, sargability, preserving semantics in a rewrite, physical design, scaling judgement
questions.technologies: PostgreSQL 16 (warehouse equivalents in the follow-ups)

sections.scenario: trip_status_events records every status change of every trip: about 2 billion rows a year, range-partitioned by month on event_ts (scenario assumption). The ops dashboard query below takes 40+ minutes. It is meant to answer one question: per city, how many trips have a current (latest) status of completed, where that latest event happened on 2026-09-14 UTC?
sections.problem: Diagnose every performance problem, and any correctness problem, in the query and its plan. Then write a faster query that answers the stated question correctly, and name the indexes or physical design it relies on.
sections.sample:
CREATE TABLE trip_status_events (
  trip_id   BIGINT NOT NULL,
  city_id   INT    NOT NULL,
  status    TEXT   NOT NULL,     -- requested | accepted | completed | cancelled | refunded ...
  event_ts  TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL
) PARTITION BY RANGE (event_ts);  -- monthly partitions tse_2026_08, tse_2026_09, tse_2026_10, ...

-- The slow query
SELECT e.city_id, count(*) AS completed_trips
FROM trip_status_events e
WHERE date_trunc('day', e.event_ts AT TIME ZONE 'UTC') = DATE '2026-09-14'
  AND e.status = 'completed'
  AND e.event_ts = (SELECT max(e2.event_ts)
                    FROM trip_status_events e2
                    WHERE e2.trip_id = e.trip_id)
GROUP BY e.city_id;

        ->  Append
              ->  Seq Scan on tse_2026_08 e_1
                    Filter: ((status = 'completed') AND (date_trunc('day', (event_ts AT TIME ZONE 'UTC')) = '2026-09-14'::date)
                             AND (event_ts = (SubPlan 1)))
                    SubPlan 1
                      ->  Aggregate
                            ->  Append
                                  ->  Seq Scan on tse_2026_08 e2_1  Filter: (trip_id = e_1.trip_id)

The original query returns 20 → 3 on this data. Explain why.
sections.constraints: Keep the semantics exactly as stated. You may add indexes, but you may not change the partitioning key.
sections.clarifications: Is "latest" over the trip's whole history, or only that day? What happens when two events share the max timestamp? How late can a status change arrive?
sections.followups:
1. What changes when the table grows from 10 million to 10 billion rows, and when it moves from PostgreSQL to a columnar warehouse (BigQuery, Snowflake or Spark SQL on Iceberg)? Name what stays the same and what changes: indexes against clustering, pruning, and shuffle.
  2. Your rewrite is fast, but the dashboard needs this every minute for every city, and three cities hold 40% of trips. Propose a physical design that makes the query trivial: a current-status table, incremental maintenance, or materialized aggregates. Say how it handles the hot cities.
sections.criteria: Identifies that the function on the partition key defeats pruning; the per-row correlated SubPlan that scans every partition; the double count on tied max timestamps; and the semantic trap of "latest on that day" versus "latest overall". -- trip_status_events(trip_id, city_id, status, event_ts), partitioned by month on event_ts

questions.title: The shared-van game (bitmask game theory)
questions.skills: State definition, win/lose recurrence, memoization, state-space reduction
questions.technologies: Python

sections.scenario: RideCo is testing an "assignment game" to train two dispatch agents against each other. The difficulty is in the spirit of LeetCode 464, Can I Win, but the rules are different. There are n pending ride requests, and request i needs seats[i] seats. A shared van has capacity seats. Two agents take turns. On each turn the agent must assign one unassigned request that still fits into the remaining capacity. An agent who cannot make a legal move loses: either every remaining request is too big, or none remain.
sections.problem:
def first_player_wins(seats: list[int], capacity: int) -> bool:
    """True if the first agent can force a win, assuming both play optimally."""

Give the state definition, the recurrence, the base cases, an optimised implementation, the complexity, and edge-case tests.
sections.sample_and_expected:
seatscapacityoutputnote
[1, 2, 3]4False
[2, 2, 3]6False
[1, 2, 3, 4]6Truethe only winning first move assigns the 3-seat request
[4, 4, 4, 4]15True
[5]4Falseno legal first move
[1, 1, 2, 3, 5]7False
sections.constraints: 0 ≤ n ≤ 20; 1 ≤ seats[i] ≤ 50; 0 ≤ capacity ≤ 1000. Requests are distinct objects even when their seat counts repeat.
sections.clarifications: Is the remaining capacity determined by the mask? (It is, because remaining = capacity − sum of assigned seats.) Is passing allowed? What is the result for n = 0?
sections.followups:
1. Return every winning first move, not just a boolean. Then explain how to cut the state space when seat counts repeat heavily, say n = 40 with seat sizes 1–8. What is the new state, and why is it valid?
  2. Change the rule to misère: the agent who makes the last legal move loses. What changes in your recurrence, and what stays the same?
sections.criteria: Correct normal-play recurrence ("I win if some move leads to a losing state for the opponent"); memo key carries all the state and nothing redundant; analysis of 2ⁿ·n; tests include no-move and all-fit cases.

questions.title: Compaction planner for small files (interval DP)
questions.subtopic: contiguous partitioning with a cost function
questions.skills: DP formulation, reconstructing the solution, bounding the inner loop, translating DP to a data-lake problem
questions.technologies: Python; lakehouse table formats in the follow-ups

sections.scenario: A streaming job writes one file per hourly partition to the lake. The files vary wildly in size. A nightly compaction job merges adjacent hourly files, to keep time ordering and min/max pruning statistics, into files no larger than max_size MB. Small files hurt query planning more than proportionally, so a file of size s costs file_overhead + (max_size − s)². An hourly file that is already larger than max_size is left alone as a file of its own and costs only file_overhead. (The cost model is a scenario assumption.)
sections.problem:
def plan_compaction(sizes: list[int], max_size: int, file_overhead: int) -> tuple[int, list[tuple[int, int]]]:
    """Return (minimum total cost, plan), where plan is a list of inclusive (start, end)
    index ranges covering 0..n-1 in order. Merged groups must be contiguous and sum to
    <= max_size, and an oversized input must be a group of its own."""
sections.sample_and_expected:
sizes (MB)max_sizefile_overheadmin costan optimal plan
[300, 200, 600, 100, 900, 50, 1500, 400]102410000824404[(0,1), (2,3), (4,5), (6,6), (7,7)]
[100, 100, 100, 100, 100]5120144[(0,4)]
[2000]102477[(0,0)]

Any plan that reaches the minimum cost is accepted.
sections.constraints: 1 ≤ n ≤ 5,000; 1 ≤ sizes[i] ≤ 10⁵; 1 ≤ max_size ≤ 10⁴; 0 ≤ file_overhead ≤ 10⁹.
sections.clarifications: Can an oversized file be split? (No.) Is an empty input valid? Does the last file get an exemption from slack, as in word-wrap? (No.)
sections.followups:
1. n becomes 10⁶ (one file per minute for two years) and every sizes[i] ≥ 1. How do you make the DP fast enough? Use the fact that a group sums to at most max_size, then say what changes if the minimum size is 0.
  2. Move from algorithm to platform. In Iceberg or Delta, what does compaction actually do to readers and to concurrent writers, snapshots and time travel? How would you schedule it so it never conflicts with the streaming writer?
sections.criteria: Correct dp[j] = min over i of dp[i] + cost(i..j-1); handles oversized inputs; reconstructs the plan; O(n·k) bound reasoning; links the toy model to real compaction trade-offs.

questions.title: Crash after write, before offset commit: guaranteeing no duplicate business records
questions.skills: Precise semantics vocabulary, end-to-end reasoning, idempotent sink design, cost of guarantees
questions.technologies: Apache Kafka, a relational or lakehouse sink, Flink or Spark Structured Streaming

sections.scenario: The trip-completed topic carries about 50M events/hour (scenario assumption). A consumer service reads each event, computes a driver-payout line, writes it to a payouts store, and then commits its Kafka offset. Last night a consumer was OOM-killed after writing output but before committing the offset. On restart it re-read about 400k events, and finance found duplicate payout lines.
sections.problem: Explain exactly why duplicates appear. Then design the pipeline so that each source event produces exactly one payout line, even under crashes, rebalances, producer retries and replays. Distinguish what Kafka guarantees from what your design must guarantee.
sections.sample:
trip-completed (key = trip_id, 256 partitions)
{ "event_id": "uuid", "trip_id": 991, "driver_id": 42, "fare_cents": 1830,
  "completed_at": "2026-09-14T08:30:00Z", "schema_version": 3 }

payout_lines(payout_line_id, driver_id, trip_id, amount_cents, created_at)   -- current table, no unique keys
sections.expected: A design and an explanation that cover: the failure timeline; the guarantee you choose and why; the sink schema change and the write pattern; the recovery and replay procedure; how you prove the guarantee holds in production.
sections.constraints: p99 end-to-end latency ≤ 60 s. The payouts store must be queryable by finance. You cannot change producers this quarter.
sections.clarifications: Can the same trip legitimately emit two different completion events, for example a fare adjustment? Is event_id stable across producer retries? What is the source topic's retention, and how far back can we replay?
sections.followups:
1. Your sink is now an external HTTP payments API that is not idempotent, and you cannot change it. What can you still guarantee, and how? Consider an outbox, a dedup ledger, reconciliation, and what you surface when the guarantee cannot be met.
  2. Someone proposes "just turn on Kafka exactly-once". State precisely what Kafka transactions and idempotent producers do and do not cover. Then estimate what a consumer-side dedup store costs at 50M events/hour with a 7-day replay window.
sections.criteria: Separates at-least-once delivery from effectively-once results; puts idempotency in the sink via a natural key and upsert or ON CONFLICT, or via transactional offset storage; knows where Kafka EOS ends; has a recovery and replay story with a reconciliation check; talks about cost.

questions.title: CDC into the lakehouse with schema evolution and out-of-order updates
questions.subtopic: CDC, schema evolution, MERGE, partitioning and skew
questions.skills: Log-based CDC, ordering, deletes, snapshot + stream bootstrap, schema compatibility, MERGE cost
questions.technologies: PostgreSQL logical replication, Debezium-style CDC, Kafka, Spark, Iceberg or Delta

sections.scenario: The drivers table (30M rows) in the operational PostgreSQL database must be mirrored into the lakehouse within 15 minutes. It must also keep full history for audits. Upstream teams change the schema without warning about twice a month (scenario assumption).
sections.problem: Design the pipeline end to end: the initial load, continuous change capture, applying changes to a current-state table and a history table, deletes, schema changes, and the operational behaviour.
sections.sample:
A simplified change event:

{"op": "u", "source": {"lsn": 88123344, "txId": 5521, "ts_ms": 1789374000000},
 "before": {"driver_id": 42, "city_id": 7, "status": "active",    "rating": 4.91},
 "after":  {"driver_id": 42, "city_id": 9, "status": "suspended", "rating": 4.91}}

Upcoming schema changes: add vehicle_type TEXT NULL; widen rating from NUMERIC(3,2) to NUMERIC(4,3); rename status to account_status.
sections.expected: An architecture with its data flow; the DDL for both target tables; the MERGE logic in Spark SQL or pseudocode, including ordering; and a classification of each schema change as safe, needs coordination, or breaking, with the handling for each.
sections.constraints: No double-counting in the history table on replay. The source database must not be overloaded during the initial snapshot.
sections.clarifications: Is ordering guaranteed per key, per partition, or globally? Are hard deletes possible, or only soft deletes? Do consumers need "as of" queries?
sections.followups:
1. A batch contains three updates to the same driver_id, and one of them arrived late from a replayed partition. MERGE fails with "multiple source rows matched". Fix it in a way that stays correct on replay.
  2. Ten "fleet" accounts get 40% of all updates, and the MERGE stage now has one task running 30× longer than the median. Diagnose and fix it. Consider partitioning, bucketing, salting, and merge-on-read against copy-on-write.
sections.criteria: Snapshot plus stream with an exact handoff (LSN or watermark); orders by the source log position, not arrival time; deletes as tombstones; idempotent history inserts; schema-registry compatibility modes; reasoning about MERGE cost.

questions.title: Debug the daily driver-earnings PySpark job
questions.subtopic: PySpark joins, windows, time zones, writes
questions.skills: Reading code for semantic bugs, Spark execution knowledge, prioritising defects
questions.technologies: PySpark 3.5, Parquet on object storage

sections.scenario: This job computes each driver's earnings per city-local calendar day, along with the driver's share of their city's total. Finance says totals are "sometimes higher, sometimes lower" than the ledger. Yesterday the job also deleted every earlier day of the output table.
sections.problem: Find every defect: correctness, determinism, performance and operability. Rank them by impact and give corrected code.
sections.sample:
# trips:     trip_id, driver_id, city_id, status ('completed'|'cancelled'|'no_show'|NULL), completed_at TIMESTAMP (UTC), fare DECIMAL
# payments:  payment_id, trip_id, amount DECIMAL, kind ('charge'|'tip'|'adjustment')   -- 0..n rows per trip
# dim_city:  city_id, timezone (IANA, e.g. 'America/Sao_Paulo')                       -- 600 rows
# dim_driver: driver_id, tier, valid_from, valid_to (SCD2, valid_to NULL = current)   -- 40M rows, ~6 GB
# Business rule: only COMPLETED trips count; earnings = fare + tips + adjustments.
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession, functions as F, Window

spark = SparkSession.builder.appName("driver_daily_earnings").getOrCreate()
run_date = "2026-09-14"

trips    = spark.read.parquet("s3://lake/trips/")
payments = spark.read.parquet("s3://lake/payments/")
cities   = spark.read.parquet("s3://lake/dim_city/")
drivers  = spark.read.parquet("s3://lake/dim_driver/")

daily = (
    trips
    .filter(F.col("status") != "cancelled")
    .join(payments, "trip_id")
    .join(F.broadcast(drivers), "driver_id")
    .join(cities, "city_id")
    .withColumn("local_date", F.to_date("completed_at"))
    .filter(F.col("local_date") == run_date)
    .dropDuplicates(["trip_id"])
    .groupBy("driver_id", "city_id", "local_date", "tier")
    .agg(F.sum("fare").alias("fares"), F.sum("amount").alias("extras"))
    .withColumn("earnings", F.col("fares") + F.col("extras"))
)

w = Window.partitionBy("city_id").orderBy("earnings")
result = (daily
    .withColumn("city_total", F.sum("earnings").over(w))
    .withColumn("share", F.col("earnings") / F.col("city_total")))

(result.write.mode("overwrite")
       .partitionBy("local_date")
       .parquet("s3://lake/agg/driver_daily_earnings/"))
sections.expected: A ranked list of defects, each with what goes wrong, an input that triggers it, and the fix. Then a corrected job.
sections.constraints: Keep Spark 3.5 and Parquet. Assume default Spark configuration unless you say otherwise.
sections.clarifications: Which tier should a driver get on a day their tier changed? Does "adjustment" include negative amounts? Is trips partitioned on disk, and by what?
sections.followups:
1. After your fixes, one task for São Paulo runs for 50 minutes while the other 199 finish in 2. Explain why, then fix it without changing the output.
  2. Finance wants the job to be re-runnable for any past date with byte-identical output. What else must change: deterministic inputs, snapshot reads, output commit protocol, and tests?
sections.criteria: Catches the join fan-out, the SCD2 join without validity bounds, dropDuplicates masking bugs nondeterministically, != dropping NULLs and keeping no-shows, the UTC/local date, the running-sum window frame, static partition overwrite, and the forced 6 GB broadcast. Ranks by blast radius; the fixes are minimal and correct.

questions.title: Concert and event seat booking
questions.skills: Inventory modeling, transactional isolation, hold expiry, booking history, analytical facts
questions.technologies: PostgreSQL (OLTP), any warehouse (OLAP)

sections.scenario: A ticketing marketplace sells reserved seats for 20,000 events a month. Some venues have 80,000 seats. On-sale spikes reach 50,000 checkout attempts per second for one event (scenario assumption). A buyer holds seats for 8 minutes while paying. Bookings can be modified (a seat change) and cancelled, with partial refunds.
sections.problem: Design the transactional model and the analytical model. Guarantee no double-sold seat. Preserve every historical change to a booking. Support reporting on sell-through, hold abandonment and cancellation rates.
sections.sample: Seed entities: venue, section, seat, event, price_tier, buyer, hold, booking, booking_item, payment, refund. You decide the keys, the constraints and which of these survive into the warehouse.
sections.expected: DDL for the OLTP core with its constraints; the hold, confirm, release and cancel flows written as transactions; a star schema with the grain of each fact stated; and SQL for (1) sell-through % by event and price tier, and (2) the hold-abandonment rate per event in the first hour of on-sale.
sections.constraints: Seat availability must be strongly consistent. Analytics may lag by up to 5 minutes. The audit trail is retained for 7 years.
sections.clarifications: General admission as well as reserved seating? Can a hold be extended? Are prices dynamic during the on-sale? Who owns a refund decision: the organiser or the platform?
sections.followups:
1. Two buyers click "pay" on the last available seat in the same millisecond. Walk through exactly what your schema and transactions do, compare at least two concurrency strategies, and say which you would choose for an 80,000-seat on-sale.
  2. A buyer moves from seat A12 to B7 and later cancels one of two tickets. Show the rows that change in OLTP and in the warehouse. How does an analyst reconstruct the booking as it stood on any past date?
sections.criteria: A uniqueness or locking guarantee enforced by the database, not by the application alone; holds that expire safely; a history model (immutable event rows or SCD2) with a clear grain; correct SQL against their own model; reasoning about scale for the on-sale hotspot.

questions.title: Ride-hailing trip lifecycle and driver history
questions.subtopic: accumulating snapshot fact, SCD2, point-in-time joins
questions.skills: Choosing fact types, grain, SCD2 joins, metric definitions
questions.technologies: PostgreSQL, any warehouse

sections.scenario: RideCo needs analytics on the trip funnel: requested → matched → driver arrived → started → completed or cancelled (by rider, driver or system). Drivers change vehicle, city and service tier over time. Pricing includes a surge multiplier. Volume is about 30M trips a day across 600 cities (scenario assumption).
sections.problem: Model the trip lifecycle for funnel and duration analysis, the driver dimension with history, and pricing. Explain the choice between a transaction fact, a periodic snapshot and an accumulating snapshot, and choose one or a combination.
sections.sample: The operational source is trip_events(trip_id, event_type, event_ts, actor, payload JSON), plus drivers and vehicles tables that are updated in place.
sections.expected: The model with the grain of every table; the SCD type and the tracked attributes for the driver; the late-data policy; and SQL for (1) weekly completion rate by city and the driver's service tier at the time of the trip, and (2) the median minutes from request to pickup by city and hour of day.
sections.constraints: A cancellation may arrive up to 2 hours after the trip was requested. A driver tier change may arrive up to 24 hours late.
sections.clarifications: Does "completion rate" exclude rider cancellations within 2 minutes? Which city owns a cross-city trip? Is surge a dimension attribute or a fact measure?
sections.followups:
1. A tier update for a driver arrives 24 hours late and changes which tier owned yesterday's trips. Show how your SCD2 and fact tables are corrected, and what happens to dashboards that were already published.
  2. Real-time cancellation rate per city is needed with under a minute of latency. Which part of your model serves it, and how do you keep the real-time number and the warehouse number from disagreeing?
sections.criteria: A well-argued fact choice, usually an accumulating snapshot plus an event fact; correct SCD2 with an effective date range and a point-in-time join; precise metric definitions; a policy for late arrivals.

questions.title: Food-delivery order lifecycle
questions.subtopic: multi-party state machine, order items, time-in-state
questions.skills: State machines, out-of-order events, handling multiple grains, bridge tables
questions.technologies: PostgreSQL, any warehouse, Kafka as the event source

sections.scenario: An order involves a customer, a restaurant and one or more couriers. A large order can be split or reassigned. Items can be modified after the order is placed: substitutions, or out-of-stock removals. Status events come from three different apps with unsynchronised clocks, so they arrive out of order (scenario assumption).
sections.problem: Design the operational state model and the analytical model so the business can measure prep time, courier wait, delivery time, item-level substitution rates, and refunds by cause.
sections.sample: Status events: placed, accepted, prep_started, ready, courier_assigned, courier_arrived_restaurant, picked_up, delivered, cancelled, refunded. Each event carries order_id, status, source_app, device_ts, server_ts, courier_id?.
sections.expected: A state machine of allowed transitions; the rule for building an authoritative timeline from out-of-order events; a model with an order-level fact and an item-level fact (or a reason for a different choice) and a courier-assignment bridge; and SQL for (1) P90 prep time per restaurant per week and (2) the time each order spent in each state.
sections.constraints: A courier reassignment must not lose the first courier's leg. Refunds can be partial and item-level.
sections.clarifications: Which clock is authoritative? Can an order go back from ready to prep_started? How do you attribute a refund that spans items and delivery fee?
sections.followups:
1. picked_up arrives before courier_assigned because of clock skew, and a duplicate delivered arrives 3 hours later. Show exactly what your pipeline stores and what the metrics show.
  2. Finance needs revenue at item grain and ops needs time at order grain. A naive join double-counts the delivery fee. Show the double count, then the model or query that prevents it.
sections.criteria: An explicit state machine and transition validation; ordering by server time with device time kept; grains that do not fan out; a bridge for many-to-many couriers; correct percentile SQL.

questions.title: Payments, refunds and a double-entry ledger
questions.skills: Financial correctness, immutability, idempotency keys, reconciliation, currency handling
questions.technologies: PostgreSQL, a warehouse, PSP settlement files

sections.scenario: RideCo charges riders through two payment service providers (PSPs) in 40 currencies. It supports authorisation, capture, partial and multiple refunds, chargebacks, and driver payouts. Each PSP sends a daily settlement file. Finance must close the books each month, and auditors ask "why did this balance change?" (scenario assumption).
sections.problem: Design the payment and refund model so that a retry never double-charges or double-refunds, refunds can never exceed the captured amount, and every balance can be explained from immutable entries. Include the analytical layer and reconciliation against PSP files.
sections.expected: DDL with idempotency constraints; the flow for one refund request that is retried three times; the ledger postings (debits and credits) for a charge, a partial refund and a chargeback; and SQL for (1) daily net revenue by currency and in USD, and (2) a reconciliation report of internal captures against PSP settlement lines, with mismatch categories.
sections.constraints: Amounts are integer minor units. The ledger is append-only. Corrections are compensating entries, never updates.
sections.clarifications: Which FX rate applies: transaction time, settlement time, or month-end? Who is the source of truth for refund success: us or the PSP webhook? What are the rules for currencies with no minor unit, or three decimal places?
sections.followups:
1. Two refund requests for the same capture race, each for 60% of the amount. Show how the schema and transaction guarantee that at most 100% is refunded, and what each caller sees.
  2. The PSP file shows a capture you never recorded, and you show a refund the PSP never settled. Define the reconciliation states, the time windows, and who is alerted. How do month-end close and late settlement interact?
sections.criteria: Append-only double entry that balances to zero; idempotency keys as unique constraints; refund caps enforced under concurrency; integer minor units; FX as data, not code; reconciliation with explicit categories.

questions.title: Subscriptions, cancellations and the MRR bridge
questions.subtopic: plan changes, proration, churn and reactivation, MRR movements
questions.skills: Temporal modeling, densification, metric taxonomy, real-time against batch
questions.technologies: PostgreSQL, any warehouse, a streaming source for real time

sections.scenario: RideCo Pass is a monthly subscription with three plans. Customers upgrade and downgrade mid-cycle with proration, pause, cancel at period end or immediately, and reactivate. Leadership reviews an MRR bridge every month: opening → new, reactivation, expansion, contraction, churn → closing.
sections.problem: Model subscriptions so the business can compute the MRR bridge, churn and reactivation, and a real-time cancellation rate. Then write the bridge query against the snapshot fact below, which is one valid output of your model.
sections.sample:
CREATE TABLE fact_subscription_month (   -- grain: one row per account per month with MRR > 0
  account_id  BIGINT        NOT NULL,
  month       DATE          NOT NULL,    -- first day of the month
  mrr         NUMERIC(12,2) NOT NULL CHECK (mrr > 0),
  PRIMARY KEY (account_id, month)
);
-- account: Jul, Aug, Sep 2026
-- 1: 100, 100, 150      2: 50, 50, —       3: —, 80, 60
-- 4: 40, —, 40          5: —, —, 200       6: 30, 30, 30

Definitions: new means MRR > 0 for the first time ever. Reactivation means MRR > 0 after at least one earlier active month and a previous month at 0. Expansion and contraction are changes between two active months. Churn means active last month and 0 this month (shown as a negative number).
sections.constraints: Valid PostgreSQL 16. Months with no row for an account mean MRR = 0, and your query must make those zeros exist.
sections.clarifications: Is a paused subscription churned? Is "cancel at period end" churn in the month of the request or the month it takes effect? How are annual plans normalised to MRR?
sections.followups:
1. Model the source of this snapshot: subscription periods, plan changes with proration, pauses and cancellations. Show how a mid-month upgrade from plan B to plan C appears in your tables, and where the snapshot's month-end MRR comes from.
  2. Leadership wants the cancellation rate in real time (rolling 24 hours, per country). Define the numerator and denominator precisely, and design how it is computed from the event stream so that it reconciles with the monthly batch number.
sections.criteria: Densifies the grid (a missing month is a zero); classification is mutually exclusive and exhaustive; the bridge balances; the source model handles proration and effective dating; real-time metric definitions are precise.

runner.starter:
-- fact_subscription_month(account_id, month, mrr): one row per account per month with MRR > 0
SELECT *
FROM fact_subscription_month
ORDER BY account_id, month;

diagnostics.message: Missing months were never turned into zeros, so LAG compares July with September: account 4's reactivation and account 2's churn disappear. Build a dense account × month grid first.

questions.title: Global video streaming analytics platform (primary scenario)
questions.skills: End-to-end design, windowing and watermark semantics, distinct counting at scale, hot keys, multi-region, adapting under changing conditions
questions.technologies: Kafka (or Kinesis/Pub/Sub), Flink or Spark Structured Streaming, object storage plus Iceberg/Delta, a real-time OLAP store (Pinot, Druid or ClickHouse), Redis, a warehouse

sections.scenario: StreamCo has 40M peak concurrent viewers across 6 regions. Players send a heartbeat every 10 s and events for play, pause, seek, buffer start and end, error, and stop (scenario assumption). Leadership wants live dashboards and an API that powers a "Trending now" row in the app.
sections.problem:
Design an architecture that tracks:

  1. The top 10 trending titles over a rolling one-hour window, globally and per region.
  2. Titles with the highest abandonment rate. You define abandonment.
  3. Concurrent active viewers, globally, per region and per title.
  4. Regional popularity.
  5. Real-time playback failures: rate and spikes by title, CDN, device and ISP.
sections.sample:
A starting event, which you should improve:

{"event_id":"uuid","session_id":"uuid","user_id":"hash","title_id":"t_8812","event_type":"heartbeat",
 "position_s":1530,"device":"tv_os","region":"eu-west","cdn":"cdn-b","client_ts":"...","bitrate_kbps":5800}
sections.expected: An architecture diagram described in words or drawn; the topic and partition-key design; window and watermark definitions for each metric; state size estimates; the storage and serving tiers with freshness SLOs; and a trade-off table.
sections.constraints: (scenario assumptions). Trending freshness ≤ 30 s. Failure alerts ≤ 60 s. Concurrency error ≤ 1%. Dashboards p95 under 500 ms. The budget matters.
sections.clarifications: Does "trending" mean the most watched, or the fastest-growing? Is it weighted by watch time? Does a user count once per title? Is the "Trending now" row personalised? Must per-region results stay in their region for data residency?
sections.challenges:
The interviewer injects these one at a time; adapt your design for each.

  1. Traffic rises 10× during a major sports final.
  2. Processing latency rises from 2 s to 2 minutes.
  3. A regional processing cluster fails.
  4. One popular title creates a hot partition.
  5. Late events change a Top 10 that has already been published.
sections.followups:
1. Your top-10 uses a sliding 1-hour window with a 1-minute slide. Compute the state that implies at your scale, then propose a cheaper design that gives the same answer within a stated tolerance.
  2. Concurrent viewers must be exact for the live sports final, because it is contractually reported to a rights holder, but approximate everywhere else. How does that one requirement change your architecture?
sections.criteria: Event-time correctness with an explicit lateness policy; an aggregation that is aware of hot keys; heartbeat-based concurrency with session timeouts; an honest account of the limits of exactly-once; a serving tier that matches each query; costed trade-offs; adapts sensibly to each challenge.

questions.title: Real-time marketplace supply and demand features for surge pricing
questions.skills: Geo partitioning, freshness SLOs, training-serving skew, feature store design, degradation strategy
questions.technologies: Kafka, Flink or Spark, H3 or S2 indexing, a key-value store (Redis or Cassandra), lakehouse, a feature store

sections.scenario: A pricing model sets a surge multiplier for each hexagonal cell every 30 s. It needs features per hex: open requests, available drivers, ETA percentiles and a 5-minute demand trend. There are 5M driver location pings every 4 s at peak, and 200k requests a minute (scenario assumption).
sections.problem: Design the pipeline that computes these features, serves them to the pricing service, and produces the same features offline for model training.
sections.sample: driver_ping(driver_id, lat, lng, status, ts), ride_request(request_id, rider_id, lat, lng, product, ts), eta_estimate(request_id, eta_s, ts).
sections.expected: The data flow; how hexes and partitions are assigned; window definitions; the online store's schema and TTLs; how features are logged for training; and what the pricing service does when features are stale.
sections.constraints: Feature freshness p99 under 5 s. Pricing must never use a feature older than 60 s; it falls back instead.
sections.clarifications: Which hex resolution, and is it the same in dense and sparse areas? How should a driver near a cell boundary be counted? Is the model per-city or global?
sections.followups:
1. A stadium empties and one hex receives 30× normal requests. Partitioning by hex now gives one hot task. Fix it without making the feature wrong.
  2. Model accuracy offline is much better than online. Diagnose likely sources of training-serving skew in your design and show how point-in-time-correct feature logging fixes them.
sections.criteria: Sensible geo partitioning and handling of hot cells; event time with bounded lateness; the online store matches the access pattern; one feature definition shared by online and offline; explicit staleness behaviour.

questions.title: Courier location tracking and geofence events at scale
questions.subtopic: high-write telemetry, latest-state serving, stateful CEP, storage tiering
questions.skills: Write amplification, latest-value stores, stateful detection, retention and cost
questions.technologies: Kafka, Flink (or a similar stateful engine), Redis or another key-value store, object storage plus Iceberg/Delta, a geospatial index

sections.scenario: A delivery network has 2M active couriers, each sending GPS every 4 s (scenario assumption). Customers see the live courier on a map. Ops needs geofence events such as "arrived at restaurant" and "left the delivery zone". Data science wants a year of raw traces for ETA modelling.
sections.problem: Design ingestion, latest-location serving, geofence detection with debouncing for noisy GPS, and historical storage. Estimate the throughput and storage, and design for cost.
sections.sample: ping(courier_id, lat, lng, accuracy_m, speed_mps, heading, device_ts, seq_no).
sections.expected: Throughput and storage arithmetic; the topic and key design; the latest-state store with its update and read paths; the state machine for geofence entry and exit; the raw-trace layout (partitioning, file sizes, retention tiers).
sections.constraints: The map update reaches the customer within 2 s. A false "arrived" event costs real money because it triggers restaurant handoff timers.
sections.clarifications: How many customers watch each courier? How dense are geofences? Is per-courier ordering guaranteed? Should GPS accuracy filter pings?
sections.followups:
1. Pings arrive out of order and in bursts after a courier leaves a tunnel. How does your geofence detector avoid emitting arrived → left → arrived flapping?
  2. Storage for raw traces grows to 1 PB a year. Cut the cost by 70% without hurting the ETA team. Consider downsampling, compression, partitioning, tiering, and what you must keep raw.
sections.criteria: Correct order-of-magnitude arithmetic; keyed by courier for ordering; a last-write-wins latest store using a sequence number or timestamp; debounced, hysteresis-based geofencing; a tiered, cost-aware history.

questions.title: Petabyte event lake with right-to-be-forgotten deletion
questions.subtopic: deletes, compaction, time travel, backfill, governance
questions.skills: Table-format internals, cost of deletes, layout design, compliance as an engineering requirement
questions.technologies: Iceberg, Delta or Hudi; Spark or Trino; object storage; a catalog; Kafka

sections.scenario: The company's event lake holds 4 PB across 3,000 tables. 9,000 erasure requests arrive each month, and each must be completed within 30 days across every table, its copies and its derivatives (the 30-day window is a scenario assumption; check the actual legal obligation in each jurisdiction). Today each request is handled with a manual SQL DELETE, which rewrites terabytes.
sections.problem: Design a system that discovers where a user's data lives, deletes or anonymises it on time, proves it was done, and keeps cost under control. Consider snapshots and time travel, backups, streaming topics, and downstream aggregates.
sections.sample: erasure_request(request_id, user_id, received_at, scope). Tables vary: some have user_id, some have only device_id or email_hash, some carry user data nested in JSON.
sections.expected: A lineage or PII-tagging approach for discovery; a batched deletion strategy; the choice between copy-on-write and merge-on-read deletes; snapshot expiry; an approach for Kafka topics (retention against compacted tombstones, or crypto-shredding); the evidence of completion; the cost model.
sections.constraints: No more than 10% added to monthly lake compute. Analytics queries must not slow down by more than 15%.
sections.clarifications: Is anonymisation acceptable, or must the rows be deleted? Do aggregates that cannot be re-identified need recomputation? What about data in backups and in the logs of external vendors?
sections.followups:
1. Compare crypto-shredding (per-user encryption keys) with physical deletes. Where does each fail, and what does each cost at 4 PB?
  2. A backfill of a two-year table is running when a deletion batch commits. What happens to correctness and to the commit, and how do you prevent a deleted user from reappearing?
sections.criteria: Discovery through tagging and lineage, not hope; batched deletes aligned with the table layout; awareness that snapshot expiry is part of a delete; streams and backups covered; verifiable evidence; deletes costed against query performance.

questions.title: Experimentation metrics platform
questions.skills: Large joins, metric semantics, incremental against full recompute, statistical data requirements, governance
questions.technologies: Spark or Trino, Iceberg/Delta, a warehouse, Kafka, an orchestrator

sections.scenario: 1,000 experiments run at the same time. There are 2B events and 300M exposure records a day (scenario assumption). Each experiment uses 20–50 metrics, including ratio metrics such as trips per active rider and revenue per session, plus variance-reduction covariates. Scientists need daily results with confidence intervals, and an early-warning guardrail for crashes and payment failures within 1 hour.
sections.problem: Design the platform that computes per-experiment, per-variant metrics and the inputs to variance estimation. It must handle late data and metric-definition changes, and stay explainable.
sections.sample: exposure(user_id, experiment_id, variant, first_exposed_at), events(user_id, event_type, ts, value), metric_definition(metric_id, numerator_sql, denominator_sql, window, version).
sections.expected: The computation graph (exposure dedup → user-level aggregates → variant-level sufficient statistics); the storage layout; the incremental strategy; how metric versions are handled; the guardrail stream path.
sections.constraints: Results must be reproducible for a stated (metric_version, data_snapshot). Changing a metric definition must not silently rewrite the history of finished experiments.
sections.clarifications: Is the analysis unit the user, the session or the city? What about users exposed to several variants? How long is the attribution window after exposure?
sections.followups:
1. Computing user × experiment × metric every day is the expensive step. Show which sufficient statistics (n, Σx, Σx², Σy, Σxy, …) you store so a ratio metric's variance can be computed without going back to raw data.
  2. Ten experiments target one huge city and one power user generates 10⁶ events a day. What does that do to your joins, and what does it do to your statistics?
sections.criteria: A layered, cache-friendly computation; correct exposure semantics; storing sufficient statistics; definitions that are versioned and reproducible; a separate fast path for guardrails; awareness of skew and outliers.

questions.title: When the better architecture is the wrong decision
questions.skills: Judgement, quantifying trade-offs, influencing, reversibility
questions.technologies: Any

sections.scenario: Your team proposes moving the driver-incentives pipeline from nightly Spark batch to Flink streaming with Iceberg. It would be "more modern" and fresher. Today incentives are paid weekly, and the business has asked for nothing faster. The migration is estimated at 2 engineers for 2 quarters and +$180k a year in run cost (scenario assumption).
sections.problem: (a) Tell me about a time when a technically superior architecture was not the right business decision (STAR), or reason through it if you have not. (b) For the case above, what do you recommend, and what would change your mind?
sections.expected: A decision with explicit criteria (value, cost, risk, reversibility, team capacity, opportunity cost), the evidence you would gather, and how you would communicate a "no" or a "not now".
sections.constraints: Do not invent experience (see the round note).
sections.clarifications: Is a real-time incentive product on the roadmap? What does the current pipeline's incident history look like?
sections.followups:
1. The staff engineer who proposed it is your strongest engineer and will be demotivated by a "no". How do you handle that?
  2. Six months later, product does ask for real-time incentives. Was your earlier call wrong? What did you do to keep the option cheap?
sections.criteria: Trade-offs framed in business terms, quantified; reversible decisions separated from irreversible ones; respect for people as well as architecture; honest about uncertainty.

questions.title: Cutting a $2M-a-year data platform bill
questions.skills: Attributing cost, prioritising, protecting SLOs, building incentives
questions.technologies: Cloud warehouse, Spark, object storage, Kafka

sections.scenario: The platform costs $2.0M a year (scenario assumption): warehouse compute $760k, Spark clusters $520k, object storage $300k, streaming (Kafka and Flink) $240k, data egress $110k, other $70k. The CFO asks for 25% less with no SLO regressions.
sections.problem: How do you investigate, choose and deliver the savings, and keep them from coming back? STAR for a related experience, if you have one.
sections.expected: An investigation plan (attribution, top-N spenders, unit costs); a ranked list of candidate optimisations with estimated savings, effort and risk; SLO guardrails; a governance mechanism.
sections.constraints: No SLO regressions. Changes must be reversible, or staged so they can be stopped.
sections.clarifications: Is there a commitment or reserved capacity in place? Which workloads carry SLOs, and which are best-effort? Who consumes the data that leaves the platform as egress?
sections.followups:
1. The single biggest cost is a dashboard refreshed every 5 minutes that, according to the logs, is viewed twice a day. The owner is a VP. What do you do?
  2. Six months after a 30% cut, costs are back at 95% of the original. Why does this happen, and what would you have built to prevent it?
sections.criteria: Measures before cutting; reasons in unit economics; a balanced portfolio of quick wins and structural fixes; SLO protection; durable governance through tags, budgets and showback.

questions.title: A legacy pipeline that is unreliable and business-critical
questions.skills: Risk-based prioritisation, incremental migration, verification, stakeholder management
questions.technologies: Any (the case uses cron, shell, Hive and a warehouse)

sections.scenario: A seven-year-old chain of 140 cron jobs, shell scripts and Hive SQL produces the monthly driver tax summaries. It fails about twice a month and needs a "hero" to restart steps by hand. The two engineers who understood it have left. Tax season is 4 months away (scenario assumption).
sections.problem: How do you prioritise and carry out the modernization without missing tax season? STAR for a related experience, if you have one.
sections.expected: A stabilise → observe → strangle → verify plan; how to choose the order; a parallel-run and reconciliation design; criteria for cutover and rollback.
sections.constraints: No missed or incorrect tax documents.
sections.clarifications: Are there regulatory audit requirements on lineage? Which outputs are legally binding? Is any part of the logic undocumented business rules?
sections.followups:
1. The parallel run shows a 0.3% difference in 1,200 drivers' totals, and the old system cannot be proven correct. Which one is right, and how do you decide?
  2. Leadership asks you to pause the migration for a higher-priority launch. How do you argue, and what is the minimum you keep doing?
sections.criteria: Stabilises before rewriting; incremental migration with verification; a reconciliation-driven cutover; clear risk communication; protects the deadline.

questions.title: Wrong financial metrics in production: the response plan
questions.skills: Triage, containment, communication, root cause, prevention, accountability
questions.technologies: Any

sections.scenario: On Monday you learn that the "net driver payouts" metric has been 4% too high for 6 days. A deploy changed a join. The number has already gone into a weekly finance report to executives, and into payout-forecasting jobs (scenario assumption).
sections.problem: Walk through the first hour, the first day and the first two weeks. STAR for a real data incident you handled, if you have one.
sections.expected: Severity and roles; containment (stop the bleeding, flag the data, freeze consumers); scoping the blast radius through lineage; communication (who, when, what); the fix and backfill; validation; a blameless postmortem with prevention guardrails.
sections.constraints: Actual payouts to drivers were computed by a different system and are correct. You must confirm that, not assume it.
sections.clarifications: Which consumers took action on the number? Are there regulatory reporting implications? Is the deploy revertible?
sections.followups:
1. The engineer who made the change is junior and very upset. Finance wants a name. What do you do?
  2. Which two guardrails would have caught this before it reached finance? Be specific about checks, thresholds, where they run, and who owns them.
sections.criteria: Contains first and diagnoses second; verifies before asserting; reaches downstream consumers with lineage; communicates proactively; a blameless culture with real accountability; concrete prevention.

questions.title: Data engineering vs product vs platform architecture
questions.skills: Facilitation, making disagreement concrete, decision records, delivery under constraints
questions.technologies: Any

sections.scenario: A launch needs a new "rider lifetime value" feature in 6 weeks. The PM wants it in 6 weeks, at any cost. The platform architect insists that it be built on the new streaming feature platform, which is not GA for 10 weeks. Your data engineers say the only safe 6-week path is a batch job with a known 24-hour staleness, and they worry about on-call load (scenario assumption).
sections.problem: How do you get the three groups to a decision, and what do you deliver? STAR for a real cross-functional conflict you navigated, if you have one.
sections.expected: How you surface each party's real constraint; the options with their costs and risks; a decision framework and owner; the decision record; a delivery plan with checkpoints; what you do if you are overruled.
sections.constraints: Nobody may be "steamrolled". The decision must be documented with its reversibility.
sections.clarifications: Does the launch truly need sub-day freshness? What is the cost of slipping 4 weeks? Who is the final decision-maker?
sections.followups:
1. You chose the batch interim path. Eight weeks later the platform is late again, and the "interim" job is now critical. What now?
  2. The architect escalates over your head. How do you respond, and what does that say about how the decision was made?
sections.criteria: Real constraints separated from stated positions; options backed by data; clear decision rights; a written record; protects reliability and on-call health; disagrees and commits without resentment.
